extracted.intended_audience: general readers; students and practitioners of public relations, media studies, and history
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and techniques for designing and evaluating public relations/propaganda campaigns, media events, and persuasion strategies as described in Edward Bernays's career and writings. Includes tactical, strategic, and ethical considerations illustrated by historical examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific approach / engineering of consent
rubrics_metrics.description: Use mass psychology and social sciences to design public persuasion campaigns; Bernays called this technique 'the engineering of consent'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design campaigns based on understanding 'the mechanism and motives of the group mind' to control or shape public opinion; treat persuasion as a systematic, quasi-scientific activity. Example: Bernays' explicit claim that what could be done in wartime propaganda could be applied in peacetime to organizations and people.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of third parties (covert endorsements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Covertly enlist or fabricate independent third parties to promote a client's message so it appears spontaneous or authoritative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid direct attribution to the client; present endorsements as coming from 'morally autonomous actors'. Examples: arranging physicians to recommend a heavier breakfast to promote bacon and eggs; using paid notable people to act as if promoting smoking was their own initiative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Staging media events / pseudo-events
rubrics_metrics.description: Create newsworthy public spectacles or events engineered to attract media coverage and shape public perception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan and stage socially resonant events (e.g., 'pancake breakfast' for Calvin Coolidge, the Green Ball, 'Torches of Freedom' march) to generate widespread press attention and reframe client image or product desirability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Link client interests to public interest or social values
rubrics_metrics.description: Frame a client's product or policy as aligned with the public good or important social values.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create narratives that make a client's goals appear to serve broader public or moral interests (e.g., linking bananas to American interests, bacon and eggs to health). This reduces resistance and legitimizes the client's objectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concealment of client involvement / anonymity
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep the PR counsel and/or client hidden so that messaging appears to come from independent sources or spontaneous public sentiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instruct staff not to mention the PR firm's role; use intermediaries and third parties to distance the client from messaging. Bernays often concealed his own involvement and succeeded in keeping his name out of affairs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of celebrities and influencers
rubrics_metrics.description: Place products or messages in the hands and mouths of prominent people to transfer their visibility and credibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ entertainers, celebrities, and notable society figures to model behavior or endorse themes (e.g., placing bananas with celebrities, using opera singers' mystique, or recruiting famous society women for the Green Ball).

rubrics_metrics.name: Research and expert legitimization
rubrics_metrics.description: Conduct or manufacture research and obtain endorsements from experts to give arguments an appearance of scientific or professional authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gather or create survey results, enlist medical or academic authorities, and publish findings widely to back the campaign (example: soliciting 4,500 physicians to support a heavier breakfast, then publicizing that finding).

rubrics_metrics.name: Creation and use of front groups
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish or employ front organizations or 'information bureaus' to disseminate favorable material while obscuring the client's hand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form ostensibly independent groups (e.g., Middle America Information Bureau) or newsletters to supply information to journalists and opinion molders; useful for shaping perceptions of foreign countries or policy issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Target opinion leaders to influence the masses
rubrics_metrics.description: Influence influential individuals or elite groups so they will spread the message to wider audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and persuade leaders (academics, journalists, civic figures) because influencing them will ripple down to their constituencies. Bernays: 'If you can influence the leaders... you automatically influence the group which they sway.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Manipulate stereotypes and preconceived notions
rubrics_metrics.description: Use existing public prejudices, notions, and convictions as starting points and sharpen them to guide public response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exploit familiar stereotypes and vague preconceptions rather than trying to convince people of something wholly new; bring hazy ideas into 'sharper focus' to draw people into a desired mental picture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Framing via larger narratives (e.g., national interest, anti-Communism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Frame issues within dominant political or cultural narratives to mobilize support and align public sentiment with client goals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Connect client issues to broader themes (national security, anti-Communism, American values) to catalyze media and governmental attention (example: United Fruit's promotion of Guatemala's 'Communist menace').

rubrics_metrics.name: Psychological warfare / political counsel
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply propaganda and persuasion techniques in political and governmental contexts, including influencing policy and diplomatic positions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use PR tools to shift public and elite opinion on political matters (Bernays' CPI work, advising governments, and United Fruit's campaign tied to geopolitical outcomes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Centralization, planning, and professionalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Advocate centralized planning and formal training/licensing for PR practitioners to standardize and amplify influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Promote institutionalization of the profession (university training, licensing) and planned campaigns rather than ad-hoc publicity; Bernays argued for centralization and a class of professionally trained counselors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manufacture of consent via repeated, identical stimuli
rubrics_metrics.description: Achieve mass effects by exposing large audiences to the same stimuli across media, producing consistent 'imprints' on public opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use coordinated messaging across outlets (advertising, editorials, 'scientific' data) so millions receive identical impressions, increasing acceptance without overt coercion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tactical distribution to journalists and policymakers
rubrics_metrics.description: Deliver tailored materials (anonymous reports, newsletters, briefings) directly to journalists and legislators to shape coverage and policy responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Send favorable articles, anonymous reports to Congress, sponsored journalist tours, and curated briefing materials to opinion molders as part of a deliberate campaign (example: Report on Guatemala distributed to Congress and 'opinion molders').

rubrics_metrics.name: Astroturfing / creating perceived grassroots support
rubrics_metrics.description: Simulate organic public support by orchestrating appearances, endorsements, and front organizations that appear grassroots.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stage marches or recruit handpicked 'ordinary' participants (example: selecting good-looking but not 'model-y' women for the Easter parade) so media portray an issue as a popular movement (Torches of Freedom).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of symbolic imagery and subliminal associations
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ evocative images and suggestive associations (including subliminal or metaphorical links) to tie products to emotions or fears.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create visual or rhetorical links between product and desirable or fear-evoking concepts (example: Dixie Cup campaign linking cup imagery with sanitary concerns and venereal disease imagery).

rubrics_metrics.name: Transform controversy into a cause and recruit elite backers
rubrics_metrics.description: Turn contentious topics into organized causes by recruiting respected backers and framing the issue as socially important.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mobilize prominent supporters (philanthropists, politicians, cultural leaders) to lend legitimacy to controversial campaigns (example: using high-profile supporters for the Damaged Goods play).

rubrics_metrics.name: Orchestrate journalist tours and sponsored reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Sponsor travel, tours, or experiences for journalists to shape their reporting and generate favorable coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bring cohorts of journalists to witness curated versions of events or conditions (example: United Fruit-sponsored tours of Guatemala) to influence subsequent media narratives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical posture: justify manipulation via inevitability or pluralism
rubrics_metrics.description: Frame manipulation as inevitable and argue that skilled 'good' propagandists can counteract 'evil' uses, or that plural propaganda fits within democracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Address ethical critiques by asserting that propaganda/PR is a necessary instrument of social order and that competing propagandists provide pluralistic balance; recognize this is a philosophical/moral justification rather than a neutral technique.
